name: Yara Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We keep your answers confidential. What does a usual working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Yara Reyes, 58, and I carry blocks, set out materials and clean joints at a school extension site. I came into construction after years of odd jobs, so I still ask the trained masons to check my corners. A straight line of blocks feels good; chasing a shift on a rain morning does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the brick crew that a phone cannot carry the mortar tubs, and the talk has been louder than the change. People who can turn up and finish a wall should still be paid properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I would worry about the same old thing: I have less than a month of expenses put away, and there are hardly any other building jobs close by. My partner Luis drives deliveries, but his shifts are not guaranteed either, so a quiet technology year would not make us secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting out materials and cleaning joints at the school extension site, and take the shifts the supervisor offers. I would stop buying the ready-made lunches on workdays for the first year and bring rice and eggs from home instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worn but fairly sure of what a workday asks from me. The thin pay envelope is the frightening part, even when nothing much changes with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you enjoy enough to keep showing up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the moment when we step back and the line of blocks is straight, even though I still need help judging a corner. I came into building work late after years of odd jobs, and being useful to the crew matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the lunch money go instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The few coins from lunch go toward the heating meter, which has been taking more than we planned. Our children are grown and pay their own household bills; they are not the reason this month is tight.

say: I would say **hands-on work** still needs people who show up and finish a wall.
I would ask for **proper pay** for the brick crew.
think: Our **thin savings** and variable delivery shifts leave little room for lost income.
My **few local options** make ordinary site uncertainty hard to shrug off.
do: Keep taking **school site** shifts and setting out materials.
Bring **rice and eggs** instead of buying workday lunches.
feel: **Worn**, but confident in the familiar workday and worried about pay.
S0.quote: The thin pay envelope is the frightening part, even when nothing much changes with AI.
fieldNote: Yara anchors her account in **attendance and workmanship**, although she describes herself as still learning corners and joints.
Her **household pressure** comes from low pay, uncertain delivery shifts and heating costs rather than dependent children.

steps.text: Keep taking school extension site shifts and setting out materials
Bring rice and eggs instead of buying workday lunches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that the office may order bricks with a machine, but they still need us when a delivery is wrong. I would ask the supervisor to explain any new schedule face to face rather than send another phone link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning work is not my job, yet fewer office staff may mean stricter daily targets for the people on the ground. I am a junior hand and slower than the trained masons, so they may cut my hours first if the site tightens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a paper record of each shift and the tasks I finish, starting now, so I can show the supervisor what I do. In the first year I would ask our crew representative to raise the new targets together, and I would take weekend cleaning work at the parish hall if site hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel irritated by another system I do not understand and nervous about the weekly total. I would rather talk to a person who can say plainly whether I am booked for Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new phone link if your shifts depended on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my grown daughter to show me where to read the schedule, because I have never used an AI tool and I am slow with new screens. I would still want the supervisor to confirm any cancelled shift aloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that weekend work pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The parish hall pays a small amount for cleaning after events, and I would put it toward utilities if the construction hours dropped. My daughter has her own rent; I do not want to make her our backup wage.

say: I would say **wrong deliveries** still need the crew to sort them on site.
I would ask for **face-to-face schedules** when office systems change.
think: **Tighter targets** could reach my work even while the bricks still need carrying.
My **junior place** means the supervisor might reduce my shifts first.
do: Record **shifts and tasks** on paper from now.
Ask the **crew representative** to raise new targets together.
Take **parish hall cleaning** shifts if site hours fall.
feel: **Irritated** by unfamiliar screens and nervous about booked hours.
S1.quote: I would rather talk to a person who can say plainly whether I am booked for Monday.
fieldNote: Yara sees **office changes** flowing into stricter site targets rather than directly replacing her manual work.
She is reluctant with screens, yet would ask her daughter for **schedule help** if access to shifts required it.

steps.text: Keep a paper record of site shifts and completed tasks
Ask the crew representative to raise new targets together
Take parish hall cleaning shifts if site hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a 2028 thinking machine might change the drawings quickly, but it will not lay the blocks that year. I would also say the three years before capable robots need to be used to protect workers who have done the carrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when the office changes, and the contractor may shrink the crew if buying and planning become cheap. By 2031 I would be 63; a robot that handles blocks and mortar could take even the junior tasks I rely on, and Luis cannot cover our rent alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor now for every available school site shift and keep a written list of the work I can do. In 2029 I would still take paid building shifts, but I would ask the parish hall caretaker about regular cleaning hours; when robots arrive in 2031, I would ask our grown children whether we could share housing costs if both wages collapsed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be scared enough to lie awake. I have spent years proving I will do the hard jobs, and three years is not much time to make another living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Luis before asking the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Luis that I need a plan for the rent if the building site cuts me loose. He would be unhappy about asking the children, and I would be embarrassed too, but keeping a roof matters more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would regular hall cleaning really be safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know whether a cleaner is safe once machines can work with hands and wheels. I would ask for the hall hours because I know the caretaker, not because I believe that job lasts forever.

say: I would say **drawings change** in 2028 while people still lay the blocks.
I would call for **worker protection** during the three years before robots.
think: At **60**, AI planning could shrink the contractor’s crew before robots appear.
At **63**, robots could take junior site tasks and leave Luis unable to cover rent alone.
do: Ask for **available site shifts** and record completed tasks now.
Seek **regular hall cleaning** hours in 2029 while staying on paid building work.
Ask our **grown children** about shared housing costs if both wages collapse.
feel: **Scared** enough to lose sleep over the short timeline.
S2.quote: I have spent years proving I will do the hard jobs, and three years is not much time to make another living.
fieldNote: Yara distinguishes **2028 planning AI** from capable physical robots around 2031, yet expects pressure on crews earlier.
She resists asking family for help, but **rent risk** overrides pride if both household incomes collapse.

steps.text: Keep taking paid school site shifts through the first year after 2028
Ask the parish hall caretaker for regular cleaning hours in 2029
Ask grown children about shared housing costs if both wages collapse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that five years gives us time to ask hard questions of the contractor while we are still on payroll. I would want our representative at every meeting about new equipment and staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I would be 63, and I might keep doing site clearing while the office is almost entirely automated. In 2034 I would be 66, and capable robots could clear and carry too; there is no pension amount I can rely on to replace these wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working the site now and sign the crew petition for regular meetings about staffing plans. During 2032 I would take paid shifts and ask the parish hall caretaker about a fixed cleaning evening, then check whether our rent could be reduced by moving to the smaller flat above the shops before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel angry that the warning may come while no one tells the labourers what happens to their hours. Five years is enough to ask questions, but not enough to turn low pay into a retirement fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a smaller flat mean leaving your community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat above the shops is on the same bus line and near our church, so we could still see our neighbours. If the written rent and deposit are lower than ours, I would move there; otherwise we stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What answer would you want from the contractor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want dates for any crew cuts and a fair chance at the remaining paid site work. A meeting without those answers would only give us another hour off the tools.

say: I would ask for **staffing meetings** while the crew is still on payroll.
I would want our **representative present** when new equipment is discussed.
think: At **63**, I may still clear sites after office planning is automated.
At **66**, robots could take carrying work without a known pension to replace wages.
do: Sign the **crew petition** for regular staffing meetings now.
Take paid **site shifts** and ask about a fixed hall cleaning evening in 2032.
Move to the **smaller flat** if written rent and deposit reduce housing costs.
feel: **Angry** about unclear hours, with some room to ask questions.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to ask questions, but not enough to turn low pay into a retirement fund.
fieldNote: Yara uses the warning period for **crew representation** and practical household arithmetic, not a speculative new trade.
The smaller flat is **conditional** on written costs and keeps her near church, neighbours and the bus route.

steps.text: Sign the crew petition for regular contractor staffing meetings
Keep taking paid site shifts during 2032
Ask the parish hall caretaker for a fixed cleaning evening
Move to the smaller flat above the shops if written costs reduce housing expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade should give contractors time to treat older labourers decently instead of just letting our names drop off the rota. I would tell our crew to keep asking what happens to the work, year by year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives in 2036, and I may already be doing fewer heavy shifts because my back is not getting younger. At 71 in 2039, robots may take the remaining physical work, but I cannot say we will be ready to stop earning just because the calendar says retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the site shifts I can safely manage and put five from each full-pay week into an envelope for rent emergencies. In 2037 I would review our actual bills with Luis, ask the parish hall about paid light cleaning shifts, and only reduce site days if the numbers cover food and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel less trapped by the clock, although the money still frightens me. A long warning does not make a small wage grow on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to finance retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son and daughter have homes and bills of their own, so I would not build a plan around their money. I would ask for help only if we could not keep housing costs covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your back limits work before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the supervisor which carrying jobs I can still do safely and look for lighter paid tasks on the same site. I know there may be no such opening; then the hall cleaning and a cheaper flat become more urgent.

say: I would ask contractors to treat **older labourers** fairly as the rota changes.
I would keep requesting **yearly answers** about the remaining site work.
think: At **68**, my back may already limit heavy work when thinking AI arrives.
At **71**, robots could take the remaining work before we can afford to stop earning.
do: Take **manageable site shifts** and save five from each full-pay week.
Review **household bills** with Luis during 2037 before reducing paid days.
Ask for **light hall cleaning** if my back limits site work.
feel: **Less rushed**, yet frightened by the gap between wages and rent.
S4.quote: A long warning does not make a small wage grow on its own.
fieldNote: Yara treats the decade as time for **measured earnings**, while recognizing that back strain may reduce work before robots arrive.
She rejects an assumed **family subsidy** and wants to base any reduction in site days on actual bills.

steps.text: Keep taking site shifts that are safe for her back in 2037
Put five from each full-pay week into a rent emergency envelope
Ask the parish hall for light paid cleaning if site work strains her back

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture frightens me most because our rent depends on both wages, and robots would come while I still need work. A dated staffing plan from the contractor, paid shifts while work remains, and affordable local housing would help us make real choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the labourers where a cancelled shift lands at home. At our table a cancelled shift lands on the heating meter, not in a neat chart.

headlineQuote: At our table a cancelled shift lands on the heating meter, not in a neat chart.
portrait: Yara is a **58-year-old junior** site worker who left school early and still learns from trained masons.
She values **steady work** and direct talk, and has never used an AI tool.
With **less than one month** saved, her wages and Luis’s variable delivery shifts barely cover housing and heat.
She seeks **crew representation** and extra cleaning hours, while treating family help as a last resort.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** leaves Yara little time before planning AI pressures the crew and capable robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **dated staffing plan**, continuing paid shifts, and housing costs low enough to protect the rent.
